name: New Zealand
traditionNote: A Westminster common-law system: the binding law is in Acts of Parliament plus judge-made precedent, so you almost always need both the consolidated statute and the cases interpreting it.
summary: Parliament (a single chamber, the House of Representatives) makes primary legislation, and Ministers and agencies make secondary legislation under powers Parliament delegates. Acts and PCO-drafted secondary legislation are published by the Parliamentary Counsel Office on the New Zealand Legislation website, which since 2014-2016 carries genuinely official electronic versions - a version is official if the New Zealand Coat of Arms appears on it, in HTML or PDF alike, and courts take judicial notice of it. Other official notices, appointments and much agency-made secondary legislation appear instead in the New Zealand Gazette. Commencement is whatever the Act itself says: on assent, on a stated date, or by Order in Council, so the front matter of the Act is the only reliable answer. There is no single codified constitution - constitutional rules are spread across ordinary statutes, the common law, Te Tiriti o Waitangi and unwritten convention.
hierarchy: Acts of Parliament, including constitutional statutes such as the Constitution Act 1986 and the New Zealand Bill of Rights Act 1990 (Parliament is supreme; no entrenched higher law struck down by courts)
Secondary legislation made under an Act (regulations, Orders in Council, rules, notices)
Tertiary legislation and instruments made under secondary legislation
Common law and equity - binding precedent descending from the Supreme Court, Court of Appeal and High Court
Local authority bylaws and district plans made under statutory authority
Constitutional conventions and the principles of Te Tiriti o Waitangi, which bind politically or bind legally only where a statute or the courts give them effect

gazette.name: New Zealand Gazette
gazette.authority: Government Digital Delivery Agency, Public Service Commission (took over from the Department of Internal Affairs in March 2026)
gazette.coverage: Published since the 1840s; the website holds notices from 2000 onward, with PDFs of full issues 2000-2017 and continuous online publication since October 2017
gazette.desc: The official newspaper of record. It carries notices that legislation requires to be published - appointments, land notices, bankruptcies, commercial notifications, and a large amount of agency-made secondary legislation that never appears on the legislation website.
gazette.howto: Use Find a notice to filter by keyword, year, date range, notice number, notice type, or the empowering Act. Notices published 1993-1999 are not online and must be requested from the Gazette Office or the National Library.
gazette.note: The Legislation Act 2019 renamed the old 'Delegated Legislation' notice category to 'Secondary Legislation', so older searches by category behave differently.

constitution.name: Constitution Act 1986
constitution.authority: Parliamentary Counsel Office (Te Tari Tohutohu Paremata)
constitution.coverage: 1986-present, consolidated to the current date with a full version history
constitution.desc: The closest thing New Zealand has to a constitutional instrument: it gathers the core provisions on the Sovereign and Governor-General, the House of Representatives, the executive and the judiciary. It is an ordinary Act, amendable like any other, and it is not the whole constitution.
constitution.howto: Open the latest consolidated version and check that the Coat of Arms is displayed - that is what makes the version official. Use the version-history control to see the text as it stood on any earlier date.
constitution.note: Read alongside the New Zealand Bill of Rights Act 1990, the Electoral Act 1993, the Senior Courts Act 2016, Te Tiriti o Waitangi and the Cabinet Manual - no one document is the constitution.

sources.name: New Zealand Legislation
sources.authority: Parliamentary Counsel Office (Te Tari Tohutohu Paremata)
sources.coverage: All in-force Acts and PCO-drafted secondary legislation, consolidated and kept current, plus as-enacted and repealed/revoked versions and Bills
sources.desc: The primary destination for statutes and regulations. It holds official consolidated text, historical point-in-time versions, Bills, and Amendment Papers, and it is the only place where you get an electronic version a court will accept without further proof.
sources.howto: Use Search and browse to browse Acts, Bills or secondary legislation by title or year, or to browse all in-force legislation by administering agency. Advanced search is required to reach repealed Acts and revoked or as-made secondary legislation.
sources.note: Bulk download of the whole corpus is not offered; the API requires a free key and is rate limited.

sources.name: Parliamentary Counsel Office - Accessing online legislation
sources.coverage: Current guidance, plus background on the Legislation Act 2019 regime in force since 28 October 2021
sources.desc: The publisher explaining its own product: what is on the legislation website, how often it is updated, how official status was conferred, and what the Legislation Act 2019 changed for secondary legislation. The companion page legislation.govt.nz/howitworks.aspx sets out the same official-version test for site users.
sources.howto: Start here when you need to justify or date the official status of an electronic version - PDFs bearing the Coat of Arms became official in 2014 and HTML versions on 5 January 2015 - or to understand why some secondary legislation is not on the legislation website at all.

sources.name: New Zealand Parliament - Bills (proposed laws)
sources.authority: Office of the Clerk of the House of Representatives
sources.coverage: Current and previous Bills, Amendment Papers, and proposed members' bills in the ballot
sources.desc: Tracks Bills through each stage - introduction, readings, select committee, committee of the whole House, royal assent - and links the successive printed versions of each Bill.
sources.howto: Filter by the Current tab for Bills before the House, or search by Bill title. The Papers tab holds Amendment Papers (formerly Supplementary Order Papers).

sources.name: Hansard - New Zealand Parliament debates
sources.authority: Office of the Clerk of the House of Representatives
sources.coverage: The official record of debates has been kept continuously since 9 July 1867; the online transcripts cover recent Parliaments
sources.desc: The verbatim record of what was said in the House. This is where you find the minister's explanation of a clause, and the debate on each reading of a Bill.
sources.howto: Search by keyword or open a sitting date, then jump to the debate on the Bill you are interested in. Older volumes not on this site are held in library and digitised collections.

sources.name: New Zealand Legislation Disclosure Statements
sources.authority: Parliamentary Counsel Office (publishing on behalf of the responsible departments)
sources.coverage: Government Bills and substantive Amendment Papers introduced since 29 July 2013, with limited exceptions
sources.desc: Departmental statements explaining how a Bill was developed, its policy objectives, and any unusual or significant powers it contains. The fastest way to understand why a provision exists.
sources.howto: Use the separate tabs for Bills, Amendment Papers and older Supplementary Order Papers. Because Bills change during their passage, check the Amendment Paper tab for updated statements.

sources.name: Judicial Decisions Online
sources.authority: Ministry of Justice (Te Tahu o te Ture)
sources.coverage: Senior Courts (Supreme Court, Court of Appeal, High Court) and specialist courts - Employment Court, Maori Land Court and Maori Appellate Court, Environment Court
sources.desc: The government's searchable database of judgments. Decisions are generally posted after delivery to the parties, and no earlier than three days after they are given.
sources.howto: Fill in one or more of the search boxes - filling several means results must match all of them. Enclose a phrase in quotation marks for an exact match. The short address jdo.justice.govt.nz redirects here.
sources.note: Not every judgment is published; the database is a large selection, not a complete record of every decision made.

sources.name: Courts of New Zealand - Judgments
sources.coverage: All Supreme Court judgments; Court of Appeal from 2003; High Court from 2005; a representative sample from the District Courts and special jurisdictions
sources.desc: The judiciary's own site, with case synopses, reserved-judgment information and judgments of particular public interest. It is the place to watch for new decisions rather than to do retrospective research.
sources.howto: Browse by court, or subscribe to the RSS feed or mailing list for new judgments. Items of public interest stay on the site for 90 days after delivery, then move to JDO or NZLII.

sources.name: New Zealand Legal Information Institute (NZLII)
sources.authority: University of Otago Faculty of Law and the Australasian Legal Information Institute (AustLII), funded by the New Zealand Law Foundation
sources.coverage: Over 240 databases of New Zealand court and tribunal decisions, consolidated Acts and regulations, and law journals; deeper historically than the government databases
sources.desc: Free, anonymous, and where practitioners actually go for older or obscure judgments and tribunal decisions that never reached JDO. Also mirrors legislation, though not as the official version.
sources.howto: Use the Databases page to pick a court or tribunal series, or run a full-text search across everything. Also reachable at nzlii.austlii.edu.au.
sources.note: Not official. Legislation reproduced here is a convenience copy - cite the Coat-of-Arms version on legislation.govt.nz instead.

sources.name: New Zealand Law Reports
sources.authority: New Zealand Council of Law Reporting, in partnership with LexisNexis
sources.coverage: Reported judgments of the Supreme Court, Court of Appeal and High Court
sources.desc: The traditional series of reported judgments, with headnotes and court-ready pagination. Cited as [year] NZLR; still the preferred citation in argument even though the free databases hold the same texts.
sources.howto: Search by case name or citation on the Council's site and buy the individual PDF, or use a LexisNexis subscription. The unreported text of the same judgment is free on JDO or NZLII.
sources.note: Privately published and charged per report; the Council of Law Reporting is an independent body, not a government publisher.

sources.name: Treaty of Waitangi Act 1975, Schedule 1 - the Treaty texts
sources.coverage: The Maori and English texts as set out in the statute; the Maori text in the schedule was substituted on 6 January 1986
sources.desc: The statutory rendering of both texts of Te Tiriti o Waitangi. The Act itself records that the English text differs from the Maori text - a difference at the centre of most Treaty litigation and every Waitangi Tribunal inquiry.
sources.howto: Open Schedule 1 of the Act for the two texts side by side, or open the whole Act to read them in the context of the Tribunal's jurisdiction.
sources.note: This is the text as scheduled to a 1975 statute, not a facsimile of the 1840 sheets - for those, see Archives New Zealand.

sources.name: Waitangi Tribunal
sources.authority: Waitangi Tribunal (a standing commission of inquiry constituted under the Treaty of Waitangi Act 1975)
sources.coverage: Tribunal reports and inquiry records from 1975 onward, indexed by Wai number, year, inquiry type and district
sources.desc: Reports on claims that Crown legislation, policy or action breaches the principles of the Treaty. Its findings are recommendations rather than binding orders, but they are the deepest official record of Crown-Maori legal history.
sources.howto: Browse Publications by Wai number, year, inquiry or district, or use Search Inquiry Documents to reach the evidence and submissions filed in a particular inquiry.

sources.name: Archives New Zealand - Te Tiriti o Waitangi
sources.native: Te Rua Mahara o te Kawanatanga
sources.authority: Archives New Zealand, Department of Internal Affairs
sources.coverage: The nine original 1840 Tiriti sheets (eight in te reo Maori, one - the Waikato sheet - in English), with sheet-by-sheet detail and signatures
sources.desc: The statutory guardian of the original documents. Go here for the physical sheets and their signatories rather than the statutory transcription, and for the two other founding documents held with them.
sources.howto: Open the sheets-and-signatures pages for high-resolution images and per-sheet detail. The originals are on public display in the He Tohu exhibition at the National Library in Wellington, alongside He Whakaputanga (1835) and the 1893 Women's Suffrage Petition.

sources.name: Cabinet Manual
sources.authority: Cabinet Office, Department of the Prime Minister and Cabinet (DPMC)
sources.coverage: Current edition is the Cabinet Manual 2023; earlier editions including 2017 remain online
sources.desc: Where the unwritten part of the constitution is written down: the roles of the Governor-General and Ministers, government formation after an election, Cabinet decision-making, and how legislation is developed. Its introduction is the standard official account of New Zealand's constitutional arrangements.
sources.howto: Read chapter by chapter in HTML or download the full 2023 PDF. Substantial updates between editions are folded into the online version rather than reprinted.
sources.note: Authoritative guidance and a record of convention, not enforceable legislation.

sources.name: New Zealand Treaties Online
sources.authority: Ministry of Foreign Affairs and Trade (Manatu Aorere)
sources.coverage: Treaties New Zealand is party to or is becoming party to, including those under negotiation and awaiting ratification, plus a separate register of non-binding arrangements
sources.desc: MFAT is the national treaty repository, and this is its public face. Records adherence and entry-into-force status as well as the text.
sources.howto: Quick-search by treaty title from the homepage, or use Advanced search to filter by party, adherence and status. Select entries to download a combined PDF report.
sources.note: Not exhaustive for arrangements - minor, technical, and commercially sensitive ones are withheld, and some older entries only cite the UN or League of Nations treaty series rather than attaching text.

sources.name: Te Aka Matua o te Ture
sources.authority: Te Aka Matua o te Ture / Law Commission, an independent Crown entity
sources.coverage: Over 150 law reform projects since 1987, with issues papers, final reports and government responses
sources.desc: Independent reviews of areas of law, each with a detailed statement of the existing law before the recommendations. Often the best free explanation of how a tangled area of New Zealand law currently works.
sources.howto: Filter publications by project, topic, status or date range. A completed project usually gives you an issues paper, the final report, and the government's response.
sources.note: Recommendations only - they are not law unless and until Parliament enacts them.

sources.name: Local Government Information Portal - Council Profiles
sources.authority: Department of Internal Affairs (Te Tari Taiwhenua)
sources.coverage: All 78 local authorities - 67 territorial authorities including Auckland Council, plus regional councils and unitary authorities
sources.desc: The official directory of every council, by name, region and type. There is no national register of bylaws, so this is the practical starting point for finding the council whose bylaws apply and following the link to its own site.
sources.howto: Pick the council by name, region or type, then go to that council's own website for its bylaws, district plan and long-term plan. The contact list is also downloadable as CSV or XML.
sources.note: The portal explains the bylaw-making framework but does not host the bylaws themselves.

findLaw.task: Find the current text of an Act of Parliament
findLaw.steps: Search or browse by title on the New Zealand Legislation site and open the latest version. Confirm the New Zealand Coat of Arms is displayed on the page or PDF - that is what makes the version official and gives it judicial notice in court.

findLaw.task: See what has changed, or read the Act as it stood on a past date
findLaw.steps: On the Act's page use the version-history control to pick a point-in-time version, and read the amendment notes at the end of each provision. For amendments not yet consolidated, check the keep-up-to-date pages and the recently enacted Acts listing.

Search Judicial Decisions Online for Senior Court and specialist court decisions by party name, citation, court or date; quote a phrase for an exact match. If the judgment is old, unreported or from a tribunal, search NZLII instead, which goes back further.

findLaw.task: Find regulations and other secondary legislation
findLaw.steps: Browse secondary legislation on the legislation site by title, year, or administering agency - PCO-drafted regulations and Orders in Council are there in full. Secondary legislation drafted by other agencies is often only notified in the New Zealand Gazette, so search there by empowering Act if it is missing.
findLaw.source: New Zealand Legislation and New Zealand Gazette

findLaw.task: Follow a Bill through Parliament and find out why a clause exists
findLaw.steps: Open the Bill on bills.parliament.nz to see its stage, its successive printed versions and the select committee report. Then read the departmental disclosure statement for the policy objectives and any unusual powers, and Hansard for the debate on each reading.

findLaw.task: Find a local bylaw or district plan
findLaw.steps: There is no national bylaw register. Identify the territorial or regional authority for the area in the Department of Internal Affairs council directory, then go to that council's own website, where its bylaws and district plan are published.
findLaw.source: Local Government Information Portal - Council Profiles

findLaw.task: Read the two texts of Te Tiriti o Waitangi
findLaw.steps: Open Schedule 1 of the Treaty of Waitangi Act 1975 for the Maori and English texts as scheduled to the statute. For the physical 1840 sheets and their signatories, use the Archives New Zealand Treaty pages instead.

subnational: New Zealand is a unitary state - there is no state or provincial legislature, and only Parliament makes primary legislation. Local law exists as bylaws, district plans and regional plans made by 78 local authorities under powers delegated by statutes such as the Local Government Act 2002 and the Resource Management Act 1991. Each council publishes its own instruments on its own website; there is no consolidated national register of bylaws, and the Department of Internal Affairs council directory is the practical index. Some council-made instruments now count as secondary legislation under the Legislation Act 2019 and so must be published and notified, but they are still not gathered in one place.
caveats: Only versions displaying the New Zealand Coat of Arms are official; anything on the legislation site without it, and every copy on NZLII, AustLII or a commercial database, is a convenience text. Consolidated text and as-enacted text are different documents - the consolidated version silently absorbs amendments, so for a dispute about what the law was on a given date use the point-in-time version, not the current one. Roughly 7,500-10,000 secondary legislation instruments are made each year by around 100 agencies and local authorities, and much of it is not on the legislation website at all: the Gazette or the agency's own site may be the only publication, and some of it has historically not been published in machine-readable form. Most legislation is enacted in English only, but a small number of Acts are bilingual - in Te Ture mo Te Reo Maori 2016 the two versions are of equal authority and the Maori version prevails in a conflict - so never assume the English text is the operative one without checking the Act's own interpretation provision. The New Zealand Law Reports are privately published and charged for, and bulk access to the legislation corpus is not offered, only a rate-limited API that requires registration.
